Reading the Shape of the Graph**
Think with me about what you see in Fig. 2.2. IPD ranges smoothly from about 50 to 76 mm with every intermediate value present, and most people cluster around 62-63 mm with fewer at the extremes. That smooth bell-shaped curve is the classic signature of a quantitative trait that can take any value in a range.
Final answer: continuous (variation).

walkthrough:
Why Many Genes Means a Smooth Curve**
A single gene with two alleles would give you two or three distinct groups. Here you get a continuum, so picture many different genes each contributing a small amount to bone growth and face width. Their effects add together, so inheriting more growth-promoting alleles shifts you a little higher up the range.

Adding the Environment**
Genes set the potential, but the actual phenotype is genes plus environment. Facial bone growth happens over years in the womb and childhood, so nutrition, age, disease, parasites, chemicals or alcohol in utero can all alter gene expression or growth. That is why even people with similar genotypes can have different IPD.

Putting Suggest and Explain Together**
You need to state the polygenic idea and then explain the mechanism: many genes, additive interaction, plus significant environmental modification of expression and development. A named example like diet or disease makes the environmental point concrete.

Final answer: IPD controlled by many / several genes with additive effect / interacting gene products; environment has large effect on gene expression / phenotype, e.g. age, diet, disease, parasites, chemicals / mutagens, alcohol in utero affecting development / growth.

walkthrough:
Naming the Controller**
PAX3 does not code for an eye structure itself. It codes for a protein that controls other genes, so we call it a regulatory gene. That is the essential vocabulary for the first mark.

PAX3 Protein as a Transcription Factor**
The PAX3 protein acts as a transcription factor, also called an activator or inducer. Think of it as a molecular switch made in the cytoplasm that moves into the nucleus to find its target genes.

How Switching On Works**
The factor binds to a specific DNA sequence, the promoter or enhancer region next to a target gene. By sitting there it helps RNA polymerase attach and start transcription, so more mRNA and then more protein is made from those developmental genes. Less PAX3 protein means less stimulation, so expression falls.

Final answer: regulatory / regulator gene; codes for transcription factor / activator protein; protein binds to promoter / enhancer DNA of target genes and stimulates / helps RNA polymerase binding / transcription.

walkthrough:
Starting With the Message**
If a gene is switched on, the cell contains its mRNA. So you first extract total mRNA from embryonic cells where PAX3 is active. No mRNA means that gene is off in that cell.

Making a Stable Labelled Copy**
 mRNA is fragile, so you use reverse transcriptase to make single-stranded cDNA copies. During synthesis you incorporate a fluorescent label, dye or tag. Now each cDNA molecule glows and represents one originally expressed gene.

The Microarray Chip**
The chip is a glass slide with thousands of spots, each spot containing many copies of single-stranded DNA from one known gene. Think of it as a library of all the genes you want to test.

Hybridisation**
You wash the labelled cDNA over the chip. Where the cDNA finds its complementary probe it base pairs and sticks. Then you wash off excess unbound DNA so only true matches remain.

Reading Expression**
You scan with UV / laser light. A fluorescent spot lights up where binding occurred, telling you that gene was switched on. The brightness / intensity gives a quantitative measure of how strongly it was expressed.

Final answer: extract total mRNA from embryonic cells expressing PAX3; make labelled cDNA / ssDNA from mRNA using reverse transcriptase and fluorescent nucleotides / dye; microarray / chip carries single-stranded DNA probes / spots for known genes; labelled cDNA hybridises / complementary base pairs to probes, wash off excess; fluorescent spots / laser scan shows which genes expressed, intensity gives quantitative measure.

walkthrough:
One Switch, Many Targets**
This is the power of regulation. PAX3 is not one brick in the face, it is the foreman controlling many other developmental genes. A small difference in this one gene is amplified into many big downstream differences.

Level of Expression Matters**
It is not just which genes are present, both species have PAX3, but how much and when they are expressed. Higher PAX3 protein in chimp embryos drives a different level, magnitude and pattern of expression of those target genes for facial development.

Linking to the Face You See**
You were told less PAX3 in humans gives wide-set eyes, IPD 70 mm or more. Logically, more PAX3 in chimps pushes development the other way, giving closer-set eyes and narrower face width as seen in Fig. 2.3. That explains how very similar genomes build very different faces.

Final answer: small genetic difference in one regulatory gene PAX3 has large phenotypic effect because PAX3 controls / regulates many other genes; different level / pattern of expression of downstream genes; higher PAX3 expression in chimps decreases IPD / makes eyes closer together / narrows face, explaining different facial structure despite similar DNA.
